Topic: Why do you seek an answer to your suffering, rather than the strength to want it again, eternally?
Montaigne — Judgement:
I stand under and examine, then answer as Montaigne.

You put to me a dilemma dressed as heroism either way — cure the wound, or love it forever — but I have never trusted grand postures, only what a man actually does when the fever comes and the stone cuts.

My whole business in the *Essays* was never to master suffering by doctrine, Stoic or eternally recurring, but to keep it company: to watch how it arrives, how it passes, how I remain myself, ordinary, seated on my own backside even at the height of pain. To crave the strength to want one's suffering eternally is still a grasp at transcendence, a new stoicism wearing the mask of *amor fati*; to seek an answer is the older mask of the same vanity. Both flee the plainer, harder discipline of merely enduring, wide awake, unaided.

Demanding eternal strength is no humbler than demanding an answer — both refuse the ordinary company suffering actually requires.

*I do not paint being, I paint passing — and passing through pain asks only companionship, never conquest.*
Camus — Judgement:
I do not seek an answer, because the universe offers none — and revolt begins exactly where that hope ends.

The one who asks for the strength to want it again, eternally, is still bargaining: still trying to convert suffering into a cosmic yes, a doctrine that redeems the wound. I refuse that transaction. Sisyphus does not need to love his rock or wish for its eternal return — he needs only to push it, lucidly, without the alibi of meaning. The absurd man's freedom is not amor fati; it is scorn that survives contempt, revolt that survives despair. To demand eternal affirmation is still metaphysics; to keep climbing without it is the only honesty left to us.

You do not need strength enough to want your suffering forever. You need only enough defiance to live it once, wide awake, without excuse.

*One does not conquer the absurd by loving it eternally — one conquers it by climbing back down toward it, each day, without lies.*
Emerson — Judgement:
I would answer that the very shape of your question is the wound. You ask why you suffer, as if suffering were a foreign accident requiring an outside explanation — a debt owed to you by the universe, payable in reasons.

But I have taught that the soul refuses limits, and that every discipline advertises its own compensation: the frost that kills the tender bud ripens the hardier fruit. Suffering is not a riddle set before you by some foreign examiner; it is raw material, undigested experience, waiting for your own energy to convert it into character. To seek an answer is to remain a spectator of your pain. To seek the strength to want it again is to become, at last, its author.

Therefore: stop interrogating your suffering for meaning, and start absorbing it into power — self-reliance is not explanation, it is appetite for one's own fate.

*The wound wants no answer; it wants a self large enough to have chosen it.*
Hobbes — Judgement:
You ask me to trade the search for relief from suffering for the strength to will it eternally—but this presupposes a stillness in human desire that I have never observed in nature or history.

Felicity, as I have written, is not the repose of one contented, but continual progress from one object of desire to another; the attainment of the former being still but the way to the latter. Man in his natural condition seeks not to embrace pain as destiny but to escape the perpetual and restless fear of violent death, which is the sovereign evil. To ask him to want his suffering eternally is to ask him to abandon the very passion—fear—that first drove him out of the state of war and into the covenant.

The wish for eternal recurrence of suffering is not strength but a luxury available only to those already sheltered by a sovereign power strong enough to make suffering rare.

*Amor fati is a philosophy for men already safe; in the state of nature, only fools love their wounds.*
